reader.title: Lynching of two Creek freedmen near Gibson Station
bases: Two Black Creek men accused of stealing livestock were hanged by unnamed parties called 'Cherokee lynchers' in one wire and 'supposed' Texas cattle men in another (A1, A7).

Both wires say two men accused of horse or cattle theft were hanged by private parties, 'Cherokee lynchers' (A7, A10) or 'Texas cattle men' (A1), with no legal proceeding reported; no wire gives the number of hangers, though both name them in the plural.

Two separately sourced wires, from Vinita (A1, A2, A5) and from Little Rock via Fort Smith (A7, A10), agree that two Black Creek men accused of theft were hanged in late July, though they differ on names, date and perpetrators.

summary.text: The lynching of two Creek freedmen near Gibson Station was the hanging of two Black men of the Creek Nation, accused of stealing livestock, in Indian Territory on 26 or 27 July 1880.
Wire reports disagreed on the men's names and on who hanged them, blaming either Texas cattle drivers or Cherokees.
The hanging drew national notice because Creek freedmen retaliated against Cherokees, and papers predicted a battle between the two nations.
According to a dispatch from Vinita dated August 3, two "Creek negro cattle thieves, named Manlay and Jones," were hanged near Gibson Station on July 26.
The same dispatch said the hanging was done, "it is supposed," by Texas cattle men who had lost sixteen cattle while driving through the neighborhood.

A second account, telegraphed from Little Rock on August 6 on reports from Fort Smith, named the men as Bill Peters and Long Monday, called them horse thieves, and said they were hanged "by Cherokee lynchers" on the 27th.
Neither account says the men had been arrested or tried, and no report of an inquest or arrest for the hangings appears in the coverage.
The Vinita report said the hanging "aroused the colored men of the Creek Nation," who accused the Cherokees of it.
Thirteen of them crossed into the Cherokee Nation, and two Cherokee youths named Cobb and Cowan were fired on; Cobb was killed and Cowan wounded in the face.
The Little Rock wire added that Dick Glass, a Creek, was killed in the fight and that a white man was reported killed.

Between 200 and 300 armed Cherokees gathered near Fort Gibson and demanded that the Creek chief surrender the thirteen men, while Chief Bushyhead and a second chief, named as Adair or Ross, held them back.
A St. Louis report of August 4 said a compromise had been reached under which the Creeks would surrender the men who killed Cobb.
None of the reports mentions any effort to identify or punish those who hanged the two freedmen.
All of the coverage found came from white papers, carrying two wire stories, and no Black-press report of the hanging was found.

The Vinita story ran first, in the Wheeling Register of August 5 under the headline "VENGEANCE. Terrible Condition of Affairs in Indian Territory-A Bloody Battle Imminent," and in shorter form in the Chicago Tribune and New-York Tribune.
The Wheeling Register version called the retaliating freedmen "black devils" and gave the hanged men's guilt as fact.

The Little Rock story spread more widely, appearing on August 7 in Chicago, St. Paul, Rock Island, Wheeling and Carson City under headings such as "CREEK VS. CHEROKEE" and "Indian Trouble in Arkansas".
Papers in Texas and Minnesota reprinted it through mid-August, the Minnesota papers under "Indian Troubles", and the Somerset Herald reprinted the Vinita text as "Negroes and Indians" on August 18.
In every version the hanging took a single sentence, serving as the cause of a feared war between the Cherokees and the Creek freedmen rather than as news in itself.
The two wires disagree on the victims' names, Manlay and Jones in the Vinita report and Bill Peters and Long Monday in the Little Rock report.
They also differ on the date, July 26 or the 27th, and on the charge, cattle theft or horse theft.

On the perpetrators, the earlier Vinita report gave Texas cattle men as the supposed hangers and presented the Cherokees' guilt only as the freedmen's accusation, while the Little Rock report stated as fact that "Cherokee lynchers" did it.

accounts.label: Vinita wire (Aug. 3-4)
accounts.gist: Two Creek negro cattle thieves, Manlay and Jones, were hanged near Gibson Station on July 26, 'it is supposed by Texas cattle men' who had lost sixteen cattle; the Creek freedmen accused the Cherokees.

accounts.label: Little Rock wire, from Fort Smith (Aug. 6)
accounts.gist: Two Creek negro horse thieves, Bill Peters and Long Monday, were hanged 'by Cherokee lynchers' on the 27th ult.

framing.detail: Wire copy under headlines such as 'VENGEANCE. Terrible Condition of Affairs in Indian Territory-A Bloody Battle Imminent', 'CREEK VS. CHEROKEE' and 'Indian Troubles' gave the hanging one sentence and treated it as the cause of a feared battle.
The Wheeling Register labeled the hanged men 'cattle thieves' without qualification and called the freedmen who retaliated 'black devils'.

conflicts.note: Each wire names two different men; no copy reconciles them. They may be the same two men under different names.
The Vinita wire came first and from nearer the scene. No opened copy reads '9th'.

versions.value: 'supposed' Texas cattle men who had lost cattle; Creek freedmen accused the Cherokees

conflicts.note: The earlier Vinita report attributes the Cherokee identification to the freedmen's accusation only.
The Mankato paper's dates are a rewrite of the Little Rock wire.
